summary: Describes an updated technique for incrementally recomputing the standard Internet checksum when part of a packet changes, updating the method of RFC 1141. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1624 fixes an error in a shortcut for updating an Internet checksum after a header field changes. It explains why the error occurs and gives two corrected forms of the update.

questions: what is negative zero in checksum
what is the difference between rfc 1624 and rfc 1141
how does incremental checksum update work
subtitle: A corrected method for updating an Internet checksum when a 16-bit field changes.

tldr.problem: RFC 1141's incremental checksum equation can produce a result that differs from recomputing the checksum from the changed header.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1624 explains the two zero representations in one's-complement arithmetic and gives corrected equations for changing a 16-bit field.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo updates RFC 1141 and recommends either of its corrected equations for incremental checksum updates.

today: RFC 1624 is an Informational memo published in May 1994 that updates RFC 1141. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 1624.

sections.title: Why Update a Checksum Incrementally
sections.content:
Routers and other systems sometimes change fields in an IP packet, such as the Time to Live, fragmentation information or a source route. Recomputing the checksum over the full header after each change can be avoided by updating the old checksum to reflect the changed field.

RFC 1141 gave an incremental method, but RFC 1624 shows that it can produce a checksum different from a full recomputation in certain cases. This memo develops a corrected procedure and updates RFC 1141.
sections.plainLanguage: A system can update a packet checksum after changing one field instead of recalculating it from scratch. This memo corrects a case where the earlier shortcut gave the wrong result.

sections.title: The Earlier Update Equation
sections.content:
The memo uses HC for the old checksum and HC' for the new checksum. It uses m and m' for the old and new values of a changed 16-bit field. RFC 1141's equation is HC' = HC + m + ~m'.

That equation is intended to adjust the checksum by accounting for the field's change. RFC 1624 shows that the result can differ from recomputing the checksum over the updated header, because the arithmetic used for the Internet checksum handles zero in a special way.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier method adjusts the saved checksum using the old and new field values. The adjustment fails in a special case involving how this arithmetic represents zero.

sections.title: Two Representations of Zero
sections.content:
One's-complement arithmetic has two bit patterns for zero: all zero bits, called positive zero, and all one bits, called negative zero. The memo explains that adding non-zero inputs can produce negative zero but not positive zero. In an IP header, the checksum can contain 0x0000 but cannot contain 0xFFFF.

RFC 1141's equation can produce negative zero in a case where recomputation produces positive zero. The corrected equation avoids assuming a distributive property that does not hold when the result is zero: HC' = ~(~HC + ~m + m').
sections.plainLanguage: The checksum arithmetic has two different bit patterns for zero. The corrected rule preserves the right pattern when a field change makes the checksum sum reach zero.

sections.title: The Example That Exposes the Error
sections.content:
The memo gives an example where a 16-bit field changes from 0x5555 to 0x3285, and the sum of the other header octets is 0xCD7A. Recomputing the checksum gives 0x0000. Applying RFC 1141's equation instead gives 0xFFFF, which the memo says cannot occur in an IP header.

Applying the corrected equation gives 0x0000, matching the recomputed checksum. The example demonstrates the boundary case that distinguishes the procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: In the memo's example, the old equation gives 0xFFFF while recalculating gives 0x0000. The corrected equation matches the recalculated result.

sections.title: Recommendations for Senders and Receivers
sections.content:
The memo recommends that intermediate systems use its corrected incremental method. It recommends that end systems verify a checksum by including the checksum field in the one's-complement sum and comparing the result with negative zero, as RFC 1071 describes. Some implementations compare a separately computed checksum with the header field, so they can be affected by the discrepancy.

Equation 3 is slightly more expensive than the RFC 1141 method. The memo gives Equation 4, HC' = HC - ~m - m', as a less costly form and recommends either Equation 3 or Equation 4. Its security considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Intermediate systems should use either corrected equation. End systems should verify checksums using the method described in RFC 1071.
